steps.name: prompt

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Ultrasound (US) is widely used in clinic for monitoring fetal health, because it is real-time and has no radiation. Recent research can automatically interpret many diagnostic biometrics from US images. 3D US has a broad field-of-view and low user dependency, so it further brings opportunities for automated solutions that give precise descriptions of the fetus.

But currently there is no solution that provides structuralized descriptions of the whole fetus in 3D US. Such a description would help the traditional local-scale tasks, like standard plane detection and biometric measurements, and also the advanced global-scale analyses, like fetal movement pattern and longitudinal comparison. So we propose to explore a new task for this goal, which is 3D pose estimation of the fetus in US volumes. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (b), we localize 16 landmarks of the fetus in fully body, and the aim is to extract the skeleton of the whole fetus and give the different segments/joints the correct torso/limb labels.

Estimating fetal pose in 3D US has several challenges, as shown in Fig. 1. First, 3D US image quality is relatively low because of speckle noise, low resolution and acoustic shadows (Fig. 1 (a)). Second, fetal pose, scale and orientation vary a lot, which causes high variation in image appearance. This makes it ambiguous to localize symmetric landmarks and it also degrades the generalization ability of automated methods (Fig. 1 (b)&(c)). Third, accurate landmark localization depends heavily on global context in the whole volume to suppress false positives, but the whole US volume is about 200 \times 200 \times 200 in size and it is very hard to digest under limited computing resources.

Related work
- deep neural networks dominant for landmark detection in 3D US
- multi-task network for fetal eye localization
- Huang et al.: semi-supervised, 6 fetal head landmarks
- generative adversarial scheme to regularize predictions with geometric/class constraints
- limited generalization, esp. free fetal poses with varying appearance
- 2D pose estimation well studied; Chen et al. adversarial joint inter-connectivity prior; Liu et al. recurrent network for articulated relationship, feature boosting
- degrade with large volume + varying poses (our experiments)

Contributions (three-fold)
- (i) first work on 3D fetal pose estimation; pose as a map -> navigation for automated prenatal examinations
- (ii) SSL framework; landmark-based registration -> case-adaptive anatomical priors, evolving label proxy; suboptimal but explicit
- (iii) gradient check-pointing (GCP) to save GPU memory; larger volumes, better localization
- extensive experiments on large 3D US dataset

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Ultrasound (US) is widely used in clinic for monitoring fetal health, because it is real-time and has no radiation. Recent research can automatically interpret many diagnostic biometrics from US images. 3D US has a broad field-of-view and low user dependency, so it further brings opportunities for automated solutions that give precise descriptions of the fetus.

But currently there is no solution that provides structuralized descriptions of the whole fetus in 3D US. Such a description would help the traditional local-scale tasks, like standard plane detection and biometric measurements, and also the advanced global-scale analyses, like fetal movement pattern and longitudinal comparison. So we propose to explore a new task for this goal, which is 3D pose estimation of the fetus in US volumes. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (b), we localize 16 landmarks of the fetus in fully body, and the aim is to extract the skeleton of the whole fetus and give the different segments/joints the correct torso/limb labels.

Estimating fetal pose in 3D US has several challenges, as shown in Fig. 1. First, 3D US image quality is relatively low because of speckle noise, low resolution and acoustic shadows (Fig. 1 (a)). Second, fetal pose, scale and orientation vary a lot, which causes high variation in image appearance. This makes it ambiguous to localize symmetric landmarks and it also degrades the generalization ability of automated methods (Fig. 1 (b)&(c)). Third, accurate landmark localization depends heavily on global context in the whole volume to suppress false positives, but the whole US volume is about 200 \times 200 \times 200 in size and it is very hard to digest under limited computing resources.

Nowadays deep neural networks are the dominant method for landmark detection in 3D US. A multi-task deep network was proposed for fetal eye localization in US volumes. Huang et al. used a semi-supervised learning method to localize 6 fetal head landmarks. Another work explored a generative adversarial scheme to regularize the landmark predictions, so that geometric or class constraints can be used. These methods are promising, but the networks often have limited generalization ability, and this is a problem especially in our task, where fetuses have free poses and varying appearances. 2D pose estimation has been well studied in computer vision. Chen et al. proposed learning the joint inter-connectivity prior in an adversarial scheme to refine the human pose prediction. Liu et al. used a recurrent neural network to distill the articulated relationship between joints for feature boosting. But as our experiments show, these methods tend to degrade when they face the large volume and the varying poses.

In this paper we try to tackle the challenges of whole-body fetal pose estimation in 3D US and to generalize landmark detection for large volumes. Our contribution has three parts. (i) As far as we know, this is the first work on 3D pose estimation of the fetus in the literature. We believe that if the fetal pose estimation is taken as a map, navigation can be generated to assist a series of advanced studies on automated prenatal examinations. (ii) We propose a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that forces the deep network to produce visually plausible pose predictions. We use landmark-based registration to encode case-adaptive anatomical priors and to generate an evolving label proxy for supervision. The proxy is a suboptimal supervision, but it proves to be explicit in conveying prior knowledge for successive refinement. (iii) We also adopt the gradient check-pointing (GCP) strategy to save GPU memory, so that our 3D deep network can generate better features with a higher resolution input under limited computing resource. GCP has little computation overhead and it makes training and inference of larger volumes possible, which contributes to better localization performance. Extensive experiments on a large 3D US dataset show that our method deals with varying fetal poses and is general, with promising results.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Featured as real-time and radiation-free, ultrasound (US) is widely accepted in clinic for fetal health monitoring. Many diagnostic biometrics can be automatically interpreted from US images by recent research. With its broad field-of-view and low user dependency, the advent of 3D US further brings opportunities for automated solutions that attain precise descriptions of the fetus [1].

However, there is currently still no solution that provides structuralized descriptions for the whole fetus in 3D US. Such a description should facilitate not only the traditional local-scale tasks, like standard plane detection [2] and biometric measurements [3], but also advanced global-scale analyses, like fetal movement pattern and longitudinal comparison. We therefore propose to approach this goal by exploring a new task dedicated to 3D pose estimation of the fetus in US volumes. Specifically, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (b), by localizing 16 landmarks of the fetus in fully body, we aim to extract the skeleton of the whole fetus and assign the different segments/joints correct torso/limb labels.

As shown in Fig. 1, estimating fetal pose in 3D US has to tackle several challenges. First, the image quality of 3D US is relatively low due to speckle noise, low resolution and acoustic shadows (Fig. 1 (a)). Second, large variations in fetal pose, scale and orientation cause high variations in image appearance, which both generate ambiguity in localizing symmetric landmarks and degrade the generalization ability of automated methods (Fig. 1 (b)&(c)). Third, accurate landmark localization depends heavily on the global context in the whole volume to suppress false positives. However, digesting a whole US volume of about 200 \times 200 \times 200 is very tough under limited computing resources.

Deep neural networks are nowadays the dominant method for landmark detection in 3D US. A multi-task deep network was proposed in [4] for fetal eye localization in US volumes. Huang et al. exploited a semi-supervised learning method to localize 6 fetal head landmarks [5]. To use geometric or class constraints, a generative adversarial scheme was explored in [6] to regularize the landmark predictions. Although these methods are promising, the networks often suffer from limited generalization ability, especially in our task, where fetuses have free poses with varying appearances. 2D pose estimation, for its part, has been well studied in the computer vision field. Chen et al. proposed to learn the joint inter-connectivity prior in an adversarial scheme to refine human pose prediction [7]. Liu et al. further distilled the articulated relationship between joints with a recurrent neural network for feature boosting [8]. However, facing the large volume and varying poses, these methods tend to degrade, as our experiments show.

In this paper, we try to tackle the challenges of whole-body fetal pose estimation in 3D US and to generalize landmark detection for large volumes. Our contribution is three-fold. (i) To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on 3D pose estimation of the fetus in the literature. We believe that, taking the fetal pose estimation as a map, navigation can be generated to assist a series of advanced studies on automated prenatal examinations. (ii) We propose a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that forces the deep network to produce visually plausible pose predictions. Specifically, we leverage landmark-based registration to effectively encode case-adaptive anatomical priors and generate an evolving label proxy for supervision. The proxy is a suboptimal supervision but proves to be explicit in conveying prior knowledge for successive refinement. (iii) To let our 3D deep network generate better features with higher resolution input under limited computing resources, we further adopt the gradient check-pointing (GCP) strategy to save GPU memory. With little computation overhead, GCP facilitates training and inference on larger volumes and hence contributes to better localization performance. With extensive experiments on a large 3D US dataset, our proposed method deals with varying fetal poses and proves to be general, with promising results.
